query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Using spark plasma sintering (SPS) with rapid heating and short dwell times under an applied pressure will allow single-phase ZrB2 to be fully densified at lower temperatures (1900–2100 °C) and yield a microstructure with reduced porosity, thereby enhancing its resistance to liquid plating bath-induced degradation compared to conventionally sintered ZrB2.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 made at temperatures above 2300 °C that typically exhibit significant porosity and microstructural defects leading to compromised strength and premature failure in aggressive environments.
generation.intervention: Adopt a rapid densification processing route via spark plasma sintering (SPS) employing high heating rates, short dwell times, and applied pressure to achieve full densification at reduced temperatures.
generation.conditions: Preparation using SPS in a temperature window of 1900–2100 °C under controlled pressure; service conditions involve long-duration (hundreds to ~1000 hours) exposure to a liquid plating bath that challenges the ceramic’s integrity.
generation.structural_mediator: A pore-free, ultrafine-grained, and fully densified ZrB2 microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The rapid heating and short dwell time of SPS minimize the time available for pore formation and grain coarsening while the applied pressure enhances particle packing, collectively enabling densification at lower temperatures. This improved microstructure reduces the incidence of defects that, under prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath, would otherwise exacerbate component failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with conventionally sintered ZrB2, the SPS-processed ceramics are expected to display a lower level of porosity, higher mechanical strength, and longer durability under extended liquid plating bath exposure, resulting in reduced failure rates.
generation.baseline: Properties of ZrB2 ceramics sintered above 2300 °C, which typically display higher porosity, reduced strength, and premature component failure when exposed to liquid plating baths.
generation.boundary: Preparation boundary: SPS conducted at temperatures between 1900 and 2100 °C with appropriate applied pressure; Service boundary: performance evaluated after prolonged liquid plating bath exposure lasting on the order of several hundred up to ~1000 hours.
generation.uncertainty: The exact level of improvement in densification and long-term resistance to liquid-induced degradation may vary with SPS parameter optimization; scalability and uniformity of microstructure across batches require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase ZrB2 specimens: one set using conventional sintering above 2300 °C and another set using SPS at 1900–2100 °C with high heating rates and applied pressure. Subject both sets to an identical long-duration liquid plating bath exposure (e.g., 500–1000 hours) and compare their microstructural integrity and mechanical properties.
measurements: Density and porosity (using Archimedes method and microscopy)
Grain size and phase purity (using X-ray diffraction and SEM)
Mechanical strength (via flexural or tensile testing)
Degradation assessment post-exposure (via microstructural analysis and failure observations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SPS-processed ZrB2 does not show a statistically significant reduction in porosity and an increase in mechanical strength, or if its resistance to degradation during the liquid plating bath exposure is comparable to or worse than that of the conventionally sintered samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Compared with temperature, pressure is a more powerful parameter in terms of decreasing the volume, tuning packing and energy state of a sample. The polymorphic transition from fcc to hcp unveiled in this work demonstrates that high-pressure can help overcome the kinetic barrier between hcp and fcc HEAs. Since the hcp CoCrFeMnNi HEA is more thermodynamically stable than the fcc polymorph at lower temperatures, the hcp phase can be retained after pressure release, and this hcp phase may have excellent mechanical properties at cryogenic temperatures. The polymorphic transition discovered in this work is by no means limited to this specific CoCrFeMnNi HEA, and we expect that this behaviour could be general in various HEAs at certain pressure and temperature conditions. Therefore, our results contribute to understanding of thermodynamics and kinetics in HEA systems. Moreover, the relative stability of the fcc and hcp phases of hard spheres is a long-standing problem in statistical physics. Since the fcc and hcp have identical packing densities and close free energy, the transition between fcc and hcp is believed to be entropy dominated. decision.trend: Early work on single‐phase ZrB2 relied on conventional high-temperature sintering (>2300 °C) which inevitably produced undesired microstructural defects (e.g., pores) and compromised long‐term integrity during aggressive liquid exposures. More recent research in ceramic processing—especially in related diboride systems using liquid-phase precursor methods—has demonstrated that alternative processing routes can substantially lower the sintering temperature (to around 1800 °C) while yielding ultrafine, highly uniform powders. These studies show that rapid densification methods can curtail the time available for pore formation and grain coarsening, though such methods have not yet been directly applied to ZrB2 without altering its single-phase nature.
decision.unsolved: The unresolved challenge is to develop a processing modification that permits sintering in a reduced temperature regime (1900–2100 °C) while ensuring full densification and minimal pore formation, thereby preserving structural integrity during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath, all without introducing a permanent secondary phase.
decision.lever: Adopt a rapid densification technique—specifically, spark plasma sintering (SPS) with high heating rates and short dwell times under applied pressure—to lower the sintering temperature while achieving full densification and a pore‐free microstructure.
decision.why: SPS has been successfully used in many ceramics to reduce sintering temperatures and minimize grain growth and coalescence of pores. This lever directly addresses the preparation limitation by enabling a densification window (1900–2100 °C) that falls within the desired processing regime, while its rapid nature and controlled pressure mitigate pore formation that can lead to failure under liquid plating bath exposure. This approach logically builds on the trend of improved processing routes observed in related ceramic systems.
